pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Your app connects to `db:5432`. Who resolves `db`, and why is that better than putting the container's IP in the config?
expected_points: Compose puts every service on a project network and Docker's embedded DNS resolves the service name to the container
the name is stable while the IP changes each time the container is recreated
no config edit or restart is needed when the database container is replaced

questions.prompt: If `db` publishes no ports at all, can `app` still reach it? Explain what `ports:` actually does.
expected_points: yes — container-to-container traffic uses the container port on the shared network
ports: only maps a host port to a container port, for access from your machine
so the database usually needs no published port; publishing 5432 mostly invites host collisions

questions.prompt: Why does the database data go in a named volume while `./app` is a bind mount? What would go wrong if you swapped them?
expected_points: named volume is Docker-managed storage, right for data that must outlive the container
bind mount is an exact host path, right for source you edit in your editor
a bind-mounted data dir drags in host uids, permissions and slower/looser filesystem semantics — Postgres commonly refuses to start or risks corruption
bind-mounting source into an image with no toolchain does nothing, which is why the app service targets the dev stage

questions.prompt: What does the list form `depends_on: [db]` wait for, and what does `condition: service_healthy` add?
expected_points: the list form only waits for the db container to start — the process running, not the database accepting connections
Postgres's first boot runs initdb and restarts internally, so the app connects into that gap and dies
service_healthy waits for the healthcheck (pg_isready) to pass, defined by test/interval/retries/start_period

questions.prompt: You ran `docker compose down`, then `up`, and yesterday's rows are still there. Why — and which command removes them? How would you watch the app's logs and get a psql shell meanwhile?
expected_points: down removes containers and the network but keeps named volumes
down -v deletes the named volumes and therefore the data
docker compose logs -f app follows logs; docker compose exec db psql -U app appdb opens a shell in the running container

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the `.env` file next to `compose.yaml` and a service's `environment:` block? How does that split keep the password out of git?
expected_points: compose reads .env and substitutes ${VAR} into the file before parsing it
environment:/env_file: set variables inside the container
compose.yaml holds only placeholders and is committed; .env holds values and is git-ignored; .env.example documents the keys

questions.prompt: Where does Compose stop being the right tool? Name two concrete things it cannot do.
expected_points: single host: nothing reschedules containers when a machine dies
no reconciliation loop or rolling update/rollback story you would bet a release on
it is genuinely good for development, CI integration tests and small single-box deployments

questions.prompt: With `condition: service_healthy` in place, does your app still need retry logic when talking to the database?
expected_points: yes — healthcheck ordering only covers startup
the database can restart or become unreachable at any time later
retry with backoff in the client is the correctness mechanism; ordering is a convenience
